(Fig. 1, top panel). EMG spasms were highly variable with
respect to their localization, duration, and intensity. In two
patients, jerky and violent spontaneous spasmodic attacks,
clinically identical to those repeatedly seen before, oc-
curred during an EMG examination. In patient 3, the EMG
disclosed short bursts at irregular intervals, synchronous
in the abdominal and paraspinal muscles, with a frequency
gradually increasing from l-2/s to 8-10/s, and with a
rapid decay after about 1 rain (Fig. 1, middle panel). In pa-
tient 5, a series of 38 consecutive spasms was recorded,
each initiated with 1-6 short burst discharges at intervals
between 76 and 122 ms followed by a tonic decrescendo
activity for up to 3 s. Bursts most often started from the
right (16/38) and left (10/38) gastrocnemius muscles and
successively spread into the neighbouring leg muscles on
both sides, and to the shoulder muscles in 12 of 38 records,
the deltoid burst being delayed to the corresponding burst
in the lumbar paraspinal muscles by 19-51 ms (mean:
31.7 ms; Fig. 1, bottom panel).
In all patients, acoustic and a wide variety of so-
matosensory, but not visual, stimuli increased tonic mo-
tor unit firing and eventually provoked spasms, often
with a jerky onset. The receptive field for a given re-
sponse largely depended on the stimulus strength, but
principally covered the whole body. Spasms in one mus-
cle were also provoked by voluntary activation in an-
other one. Such "overflow" spasms (see [10]) were eas-
ily precipitated by activation of neighbouring muscles,
but also occurred with forcible innervation of remote
muscles clinically not involved, or even with a cough. In
general, induced spasmodic activity had a more jerky on-
set and a shorter duration than spontaneous spasms.
Moreover, there was some association between the stim-
ulus strength and the characteristics of the responses.
With increasing stimulus strength, EMG responses be-
came more and more jerky, starting with synchronized
myoclonic bursts and terminating in a tonic decrescendo
activity.

Electrical nerve stimulation was most effective in pro-
voking jerky spasms with a characteristic EMG pattern:
1-3 highly synchronized bursts occurred at latencies
around 70, 120, and 170 ms and terminated in a waning
desynchronized activity over 0.5-3 s. Polygraphic record-
ings from the ventral and dorsal trunk muscles on both
sides (Fig. 2) revealed almost symmetrical and simultane-
ous activation of the bilateral antagonists in all seven pa-
tients investigated (patients 1, 3-8), and in patients 1 and
3-7 also in the arm and neck muscles. Because of their
clinical and EMG characteristics these responses were
termed "spasmodic reflex myoclonus". Motor responses
with the EMG features of spasmodic reflex myoclonus
were never seen in normal subjects or in patients with a
variety of other motor disorders associated with increased
muscle tone or myoclonic jerks, or both, such as (number
of patients in parentheses) cervical spondylotic myelopathy
with severe spasticity (n = 15), reticular reflex myoclonus
(n = 4), Lance-Adams syndrome (n = 1), Creutzfeldt-Jakob
disease (n = 3), or psychogenic generalized reflex jerks (n =
3). In three of eight patients with prominent parkinsonian
rigidity, however, small amplitude burst responses with
comparable latencies were seen. Spasmodic reflex my_
oclonus was attenuated by oral benzodiazepines in pa-
tients 1, and 4-7, and completely suppressed in patients 3
and 8.
In order to analyse further the pathway(s) mediating
spasmodic reflex myoclonus, axial muscles were simul-
taneously recorded from different levels along the neu-
raxis. Median nerve stimulation exerted motor responses
with shortest latencies in the cervical paraspinal muscles
(52-81 ms) followed by a concomitant activation of the
cranial and lumbosacral muscles (Figs. 3A, 4A, 5B) in
patients 1, 3 and 5. In patients 6 and 7, the thoracic
paraspinal muscles were the first to respond (46-68 ms)
followed by the lumbar and cervical paraspinal, and the
cranial, muscles at successively longer intervals (Figs, 3
B, 4 A). In a second task, latencies of the motor responses
evoked by median and tibial nerve stimulation were com-
pared. In the case of a spinal myoclonus, conduction dis-
tances from both stimulus sites to the lumbosacral target
muscles are about equal, but considerably differ in the
case of a supraspinal pathway. In patient 8, whose speci-
men recordings are shown in Fig. 3 C and D, the conduc-
tion distances were as follows: inion - spinous process
C7, 14 cm; wrist - spinous process C7, 74 cm; spinous
processes C 7 -T 10, 34 cm; ankle- spinous process T10,
115 cm.
Thus in the case of a presumed spinal reflex myoclonus,
the conduction distances for median or tibial nerve stimu-
lation were 108 or 115 cm, respectively. In the case of a
presumed mediation via the brain stem, the corresponding
distances were 136 and 211 cm, respectively. In patients
1, 5, 6, and 8, EMG responses in the thoracolumbar
paraspinal muscles had similar latencies with both median
and tibial nerve stimulation (Figs. 3 C, D, 4B). Moreover,

Spasmodic reflex myoclonus strongly depended on the
stimulus strength and repetition rate. With repeated stim-
ulation, EMG responses rapidly habituated and eventually
completely disappeared (Fig.5A). Moreover, spasms
evoked by either somatosensory or acoustic stimuli, and
spontaneous and induced spasms mutually habituated.
Factors augmenting habituation were fast repetition and
low intensity of a stimulus, and treatment with the benzo-
diazepines [18]. Therefore, only approximate figures can
be given. Stable EMG responses to median nerve stimula-
tion with supramaximal single pulses or short pulse trains
(5 pulses at 5-ms intervals) were seen at intervals between

Reflex investigations
As reflex mechanisms seemed to play an important role in
the pathogenesis of spasms, a variety of segmental, multi-
segmental, and long loop reflexes was investigated. H and
T reflex investigations yielded normal silent periods after
the knee jerk in all patients, and after the triceps surae H
reflex in patients 1-4 and 6-8 (not tested in patient 5). A
more detailed investigation of the triceps surae H reflex
(Fig. 6) revealed patients 2 and 8 to have the highest H/M

with desynchronization of the reflex pattern, loss of the
inhibitory reflex component normally present between
100 and 150 ms, and a considerable delay of the reflex
onset at low stimulus repetition rates (Fig. 7 A). Moreover,
if - at a fixed moderate stimulus strength - the stimulus
intervals were successively shortened from 10 to 0.5 s, the
delayed onset latency successively normalized (Fig. 7 A,
B); this does not occur in normal subjects [20, 21]. Long
loop reflexes in the abductor pollicis brevis muscle were
normal in patients 2 and 6-8, but were replaced in patients
1, 3 and 4 by a large short-latency (27-32 ms) and low-
threshold response (Fig. 8). The latter was also evoked by
superficial radial (Fig. 8 A) and digital nerve stimulation,
and was also recorded from other muscles of the stimu-
lated arm and, in patient 1, in the corresponding contralat-
eral muscles delayed by 6-9 ms.
Discussion
Our investigation of eight patients with SMS revealed ab-
normalities of segmental and suprasegmental reflex trans-
mission seemingly related to the pathophysiology of spas-
tic motor disturbances. Although clinical or electrophysi-
ological signs normally associated with spasticity were
absent in our patients, except for hyper-reflexia of the
legs, some pathophysiological relationship might be de-
rived from the therapeutic efficacy of antispastic drugs
such as baclofen, tizanidine, or the benzodiazepines [7,
11, 18, 22]. High H/M ratios in the triceps surae muscle
associated with abnormally poor development of both
low-frequency depression and vibration-induced inhibi-
tion of the corresponding H reflex were seen in two of
five patients (Fig. 6). Poor low-frequency depression as
well as reduced vibratory inhibition have been described
previously in spastic limbs [5, 13]. In contrast to low-fre-
quency depression, the neural mechanisms of which are
not yet fully understood, the H reflex attenuation to vibra-
tion is ascribed to GABAergic presynaptic inhibition [5].

An impairment of GABAergic neurons has recently been
postulated for SMS [25], and low GABA levels were re-
ported in the cerebrospinal fluid of four patients [28].
Among our patients, abnormal monosynaptic reflex mech-
anisms occurred irrespective of autoimmunity against
GABAergic neurons. However, as vibratory inhibition
was reported to be abnormal in two other patients [12, 15],
this test might provide important clues in future neurophys-
iological analysis of SMS if applied more systematically.
Long loop reflexes to the hand muscles in patients 1,
3, and 4 provided evidence not only of exaggerated seg-
mental reflex mechanisms (corresponding to clinical
symptoms in the arms of patients 1 and 4), but also of dis-
turbed transcortical reflex mediation [6]. As median nerve
evoked cortical potentials proved normal, this might be
ascribed to the central relays of the reflex loop or to the
corticospinal tract, which contrasts a lack of pyramidal
symptoms and normal corticomuscular latencies [22].
Flexor reflexes in the tibialis anterior muscle were dis-
tinctly abnormal in a high proportion of patients (Fig. 7),
irrespective of their immunological status or drug treat-
ment. Both the alteration of the reflex pattern as well as its
abnormal temporal facilitation closely correspond to ab-
normalities seen in spastic legs. This finding presumably
in both spasticity and SMS is due to impaired control of
segmental mechanisms [20]. It is noteworthy that the ab-
normal temporal facilitation of the flexor reflex contrasts
with the profound habituation of spasmodic reflex my-
oclonus (Fig. 5 A). This suggests that these two types of
cutaneomuscular reflexes are generated in different neu-
ronal networks.
Our polymyographic analysis was based on the obser-
vation that tonic firing of motor units in SMS is distinctly
susceptible to external influences which, if sufficiently
brisk or intense, cause generalized tonic or jerky spasms
[7]. The latter are termed here spasmodic reflex myo-
clonus as:
1. Their onset is jerky and violent, i.e. myoclonic, con-
sisting of a series of 1-3 synchronized, large, and rapid
EMG bursts.
2. Their end is gradually waning, i.e. spasmodic, with a
tonic decrescendo EMG activity.
3. In a given patient, their EMG pattern is stereotypically
evoked with onset latencies around 60-80 ms, i.e. it is
a reflex (Fig. 2).
The EMG pattern of spasmodic reflex myoclonus corre-
sponds to the one recorded from the leg muscles in patient
5 during a series of violent spontaneous jerky spasms (Fig.
1, bottom recording), which suggests that both spontaneous
spasms and spasmodic reflex myoclonus are of a similar
nature, at least in this case. As compared with other types
of stimulus-sensitive jerking (Table 1), characteristic EMG
features of spasmodic reflex myoclonus such as long dura-
tion, rapid habituation, and bilaterality rule out transcorti-
cal reflex myoclonus [8, 24]. The former characteristics as
well as tight input-output coupling with respect to latency,
shape and amplitude of the responses are not compatible
with reticular reflex myoclonus [8, 9]; the latter feature

also excludes psychogenic jerks mimicking myoclonus
[26]. Both cortical and reticular reflex myoclonus as well
as some of the hyperekplexias are associated with EEG
and evoked potential abnormalities, suggesting enhanced
cortical excitability [2, 8, 9, 14, 24, 27]. Some clinical re-
semblance with exaggerated startle responses (e.g. in fa-
milial hyperekplexia) does indeed exist. However, muscle
recruitment in both physiological startle and hyperek-
plexia is down from the fifth and seventh cranial motor
nuclei to the spinal cord [2]. In spasmodic reflex my-
oclonus, the polymyographic recordings (Figs. 3-5) sug-
gest a slow spread of the EMG responses from muscles of
spinal cord segments C6/7 concomitantly up to the brain
stem and down to the lumbosacral motor nuclei. A simple
explanation for this concomitant spread in both directions,
and on both sides, along the neuraxis is that the excitatory
volley is conveyed within a bilateral longitudinal spinal
cord system. A particular form of myoclonic jerking pre-
dominantly of the axial muscles was recently suggested to
arise in propriospinal systems [3, 4]. Indeed, proprio-
spinal myoclonus in spinal cord diseases and spasmodic
reflex myoclonus in SMS share several features, such as
long duration, jerky components, and slow bi-directional
spread on both sides. Propriospinal myoclonus, however,
seems to have a strong flexor dominance and a poor stim-
ulus sensitivity, both features contrasting with the spas-
modic reflex myoclonus seen in SMS.
Median nerve stimulation in two cases led to responses
with the shortest latencies not in the cervical but in the
mid-thoracic paraspinal muscles (Figs. 3 B, 4 A). This may
indicate that in these patients the brunt of abnormal ex-
citability is located in the latter segments of the spinal
cord, and one might speculate as to whether the median
nerve volley at this site is relayed to the ascending and de-
scending fibre tracts. However, it more likely shows that
the onset latency of spasmodic reflex myoclonus strongly
depends on the gain of synaptic transmission, which is
presumably highest in the spinal cord segments most se-
verely afflicted, but may considerably differ at various
levels of the neuraxis. Such a differential gain in the reflex
transmission to different spinal cord or brain stem motor
nuclei would inevitably invalidate any calculation of prop-
agation velocities of the excitatory volley in the spinal
cord. Nevertheless, this does not principally invalidate
this technique [9], as the results are fairly consistent be-
tween individual patients (Fig.4A) and are, moreover,
compatible with a second type of testing which compares
the overall conduction times with median and tibial nerve
stimulation to a gi~ien motor nucleus (Figs. 3 C, D, 4B).
An important feature of spasmodic reflex myoclonus is
its regular appearance in the lower trunk muscles of all
patients tested, and its absence in other diseases with mus-
cular hypertonia or myoclonic jerks, or both, as well as in
normal subjects. As we are not aware of any observation
of this particular type of reflex myoclonus in other motor
disorders, it may be considered characteristic of SMS and
thus serve as an electrophysiological marker, allowing one,
for example, to differentiate spasmodic reflex myoclonus
in SMS from psychogenic jerks [26]. Obviously, this marker
is independent of the presence or absence of GAD auto-
antibodies [25], but its electrophyisological appearance
may be influence by drug treatment.
With regard to the variety of mechanisms triggering
spasms and spasmodic reflex myoclonus from a wide re-
ceptive field, one might speculate as to whether stiffness,
spasms and spasmodic reflex myoclonus are generated by
142
common neural mechanisms, the differential manifesta-
tions of motor excitability being patterned by the shape,
intensity and duration of the afferent signals. Stiffness
might in fact be considered a fragment of spasmodic re-
flex myoclonus elicited by asynchronous afferent im-
pulses from, for example, skin or muscle receptors. Some
general characteristics of such common neuronal mecha-
nisms are that they are subject to a rapid and mutual ha-
bituation, and that they apparently receive convergence
form a wide variety of supraspinal and spinal sources, sug-
gesting important integrative functions. Among the for-
mer, low-threshold muscle afferents, which are strongly
controlled by the GABAergic presynaptic inhibition (see
[5]) were not as particularly effective in evoking motor
hyperactivity (Fig. 5 B) as might be expected in the pres-
ence of autoimmunity against GABAergic neurons [25]. In
fact, electrical stimulation of the median or tibial nerves
often evoked H reflexes in the corresponding muscles
without concomitant spasms or myoclonic jerks; the latter
were, however, evoked with increasing stimuli to the
same nerves or to their cutaneous branches. According to
clinical and microscopical evidence previously discussed
[22], the spinal grey matter and the adjacent propriospinal
tracts may be regarded as the prime candidates for the lo-
cus of the disturbance, the neurons in the spinal grey mat-
ter having indeed prominent integrative functions [1].
